newsitem.title: USA: Clinton expected to waive parts of Helms-Burton law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton expected to waive parts of Helms-Burton law.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was widely expected to continue to waive controversial portions of the Helms-Burton Act designed to crack down on foreign companies doing business in Cuba, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.
"That is the assumption," said one U.S. official, who declined to be identified.

Under the law, Clinton must decide every six months whether to waive those parts of the 1996 law that allow American citizens to sue in U.S. courts foreign firms deemed to have profited from U.S. property confiscated by Cuba after its 1959 communist revolution.

The president has twice before waived the controversial portions of the law, in July 1996 and January 1997. A White House spokeswoman said Clinton must decide by midnight EDT on Wednesday (0400 GMT on Thursday) whether to continue to waive those portions.

The Helms-Burton Act, which is designed to bring pressure to bear on Cuba to adopt democratic reforms, was signed into law in March 1996 after Cuban jets a month earlier shot down two civilian aircraft, killing four Cuban-Americans on board.

The law, named for its Republican sponsors Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina and Representative Dan Burton of Indiana, has been bitterly criticised by Canada and the European Union, who fear that their companies may be subject to such lawsuits.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry declined to say what decision the president might make, but said it was a "safe assumption" that foreign policy aides had recommended that Clinton continue to suspend those parts of the law.
